question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Either the principal or the senior teachers (a)/ has to sign (b)/ the transfer certificate (c)/ before it is issued. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In "either … or", the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. The nearer subject here is the plural "the senior teachers", so "has to sign" must be "have to sign".

◦ Corrected sentence: Either the principal or the senior teachers have to sign the transfer certificate before it is issued.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Either the principal or the senior teachers" is proper, with "either … or" joining the two subjects.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the transfer certificate" is proper, with "the" used before a specific document.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "before it is issued." is proper, with "before" introducing the clause and the passive "is issued".

 

NOTE

 

• Either you or he is, Either he or they are (the nearer subject decides the verb in "either … or" and "neither … nor").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Both the design and the pricing (a)/ of the new model (b)/ have impressed the customers. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. "Both … and" always joins two items and takes a plural verb, so "Both the design and the pricing … have impressed" is correct.

◦ Sentence as given: Both the design and the pricing of the new model have impressed the customers.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Both the design and the pricing" is proper, with "both … and" joining two singular nouns.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "of the new model" is proper, with "of" showing what the design and pricing belong to.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "have impressed the customers." is proper, with the plural verb "have" agreeing with the "both … and" subject.

 

NOTE

 

• Both the manager and the clerk are, Both Ravi and Sohan have (both … and, always plural).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The flight got delayed (a)/ because the sudden fog (b)/ that covered the runway (c)/ early in the morning. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Because" is a conjunction and must be followed by a clause with a finite verb, while "the sudden fog that covered the runway" is only a noun phrase with no main verb of its own for the "because" clause. Before such a noun phrase, "because of" is used. So "because the sudden fog" must be "because of the sudden fog".

◦ Corrected sentence: The flight got delayed because of the sudden fog that covered the runway early in the morning.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The flight got delayed" is proper, with the passive "got delayed" in the simple past.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "that covered the runway" is proper, with "that" introducing a relative clause describing the fog.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "early in the morning." is proper, with "early in the morning" taking no extra preposition.

 

NOTE

 

• because it was foggy (because + clause); because of the fog, because of heavy traffic (because of + noun phrase).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Not only was the venue changed at the last minute, (a)/ but the organisers also failed (b)/ to inform all the guests in time. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. When a sentence begins with "Not only", the auxiliary is placed before the subject ("was the venue changed"), and the second clause is joined with "but … also".

◦ Sentence as given: Not only was the venue changed at the last minute, but the organisers also failed to inform all the guests in time.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Not only was the venue changed at the last minute," is proper, with the inversion "was + subject" after "Not only".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "but the organisers also failed" is proper, with "but … also" completing the pair and the plural verb "failed" agreeing with "organisers".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "to inform all the guests in time." is proper, with "failed to" followed by a base verb.

 

NOTE

 

• Not only did she sing, but she also danced, Not only is he rich, but he is also generous (inversion after a sentence-initial "Not only").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Despite he had submitted (a)/ all the required documents (b)/ on time, his visa application (c)/ was rejected. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Despite" and "in spite of" are prepositions and take a noun or a gerund, not a clause with a subject and a finite verb. Before a clause, "although / though" is used. So "Despite he had submitted" must be "Although he had submitted".

◦ Corrected sentence: Although he had submitted all the required documents on time, his visa application was rejected.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "all the required documents" is proper, with "all the" before a plural noun.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "on time, his visa application" is proper, with "on time" meaning "punctually" and no article needed.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "was rejected." is proper, with the simple past passive "was rejected".

 

NOTE

 

• Although he tried hard, he failed; Despite his hard work, he failed; Despite trying hard, he failed (clause after although; noun / gerund after despite).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Though the roads were badly damaged by the flood, (a)/ but the relief trucks (b)/ managed to reach the village on time. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Though / although" already shows contrast on its own, so "but" is not used together with it in the same sentence. So "but the relief trucks" must be "the relief trucks", with "but" dropped.

◦ Corrected sentence: Though the roads were badly damaged by the flood, the relief trucks managed to reach the village on time.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Though the roads were badly damaged by the flood," is proper, with "though" correctly introducing the clause of contrast.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "managed to reach the village on time." is proper, with "managed to" followed by a base verb.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "but" is wrongly added together with "though" in part (b).

 

NOTE

 

• Though he was tired, he finished the work; He was tired, but he finished the work (one contrast word only), and not Though he was tired, but he finished the work.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The queue outside the ration shop (a)/ was such long (b)/ that people waited (c)/ for nearly three hours. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "So" is used before an adjective or adverb ("so long that"), while "such" is used before a noun, usually with an article ("such a long queue that"). So "was such long" must be "was so long".

◦ Corrected sentence: The queue outside the ration shop was so long that people waited for nearly three hours.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The queue outside the ration shop" is proper, with "outside" showing position.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "that people waited" is proper, with "that" introducing the result clause.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "for nearly three hours." is proper, with "for" used before a period of time.

 

NOTE

 

• so long that, so crowded that (so + adjective + that); such a long queue that, such a crowded hall that (such + a / an + noun + that).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The wound was so deep to be treated at home, (a)/ so the boy was rushed (b)/ to the hospital before (c)/ the bleeding worsened. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Too + adjective + to + verb" shows that something is not possible, and "so" is not mixed with a following "to-infinitive" in this way. "So deep to be treated" must be "too deep to be treated".

◦ Corrected sentence: The wound was too deep to be treated at home, so the boy was rushed to the hospital before the bleeding worsened.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "so the boy was rushed" is proper, with "so" introducing the result and the passive "was rushed".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "to the hospital before" is proper, with "to" showing direction and "before" introducing the time clause.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "the bleeding worsened." is proper, with the simple past "worsened" in the clause after "before".

 

NOTE

 

• too deep to treat, too heavy to lift (too + adjective + to); so deep that it could not be treated (so + adjective + that + clause).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

This laptop is not as expensive as (a)/ the one my brother bought (b)/ from the online store. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. In a comparison of equality, the pattern "as … as" is used, and here "not as expensive as" correctly compares the two laptops.

◦ Sentence as given: This laptop is not as expensive as the one my brother bought from the online store.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "This laptop is not as expensive as" is proper, with the negative "not" before "as … as".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the one my brother bought" is proper, with "the one" referring back to "laptop".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "from the online store." is proper, with "from" showing the source of purchase.

 

NOTE

 

• not as expensive as, as tall as (as … as); more expensive than (comparative + than).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Most passengers on this route (a)/ prefer the express train (b)/ than the slower passenger train (c)/ because it saves time. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Prefer" is followed by "to" and not by "than", in the pattern "prefer A to B". So "than the slower passenger train" must be "to the slower passenger train".

◦ Corrected sentence: Most passengers on this route prefer the express train to the slower passenger train because it saves time.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Most passengers on this route" is proper, with the plural "passengers" as the subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "prefer the express train" is proper, with "prefer" followed by a direct object.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "because it saves time." is proper, with "because" introducing the reason.

 

NOTE

 

• prefer tea to coffee, prefer walking to driving (prefer … to); would rather walk than drive (would rather … than).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The new uniform is (a)/ almost the same colour (b)/ like the old one (c)/ that we used last year. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Same" is followed by "as" and not by "like". So "like the old one" must be "as the old one".

◦ Corrected sentence: The new uniform is almost the same colour as the old one that we used last year.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The new uniform is" is proper, with the singular verb "is" agreeing with "uniform".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "almost the same colour" is proper, with "almost" modifying "the same".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "that we used last year." is proper, with "that" introducing a relative clause and "last year" a definite past time.

 

NOTE

 

• the same book as mine, the same size as yours (same … as), and not the same book like mine.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Hardly had the manager entered the office (a)/ when the staff (b)/ stopped their idle chatter. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. "Hardly" is followed by the past perfect with "had" before the subject, and the second clause is joined with "when".

◦ Sentence as given: Hardly had the manager entered the office when the staff stopped their idle chatter.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Hardly had the manager entered the office" is proper, with the inversion "had + subject" after "Hardly".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "when the staff" is proper, with "when" correctly joining the two clauses.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "stopped their idle chatter." is proper, with the simple past "stopped" and the plural possessive "their".

 

NOTE

 

• Hardly had she sat down when the phone rang; No sooner had she sat down than the phone rang (hardly … when; no sooner … than).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

No sooner the fire alarm rang (a)/ than the employees rushed (b)/ out of the building (c)/ in an orderly manner. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "No sooner" at the start of a sentence requires inversion, with "had" placed before the subject and the main verb in the past participle. So "No sooner the fire alarm rang" must be "No sooner had the fire alarm rung".

◦ Corrected sentence: No sooner had the fire alarm rung than the employees rushed out of the building in an orderly manner.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "than the employees rushed" is proper, with "than" following "no sooner" and the simple past "rushed".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "out of the building" is proper, with "out of" showing movement away from a place.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "in an orderly manner." is proper, with "in" used before "an orderly manner".

 

NOTE

 

• No sooner had he arrived than it began to rain, No sooner had the bell rung than the students left (no sooner + had + subject + past participle + than).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The children were told to hold hands tightly lest they will get separated in the crowded fair.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. lest they should get.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Lest" (= for fear that) is followed by "should + base verb", and "will" is not used with it. So "lest they will get" must be "lest they should get".

◦ Corrected sentence: The children were told to hold hands tightly lest they should get separated in the crowded fair.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "lest they get not" — the negative word "not" is not added after "lest", because "lest" already carries a negative sense.

 

• Option 2: "lest they would get" — "would" is not used after "lest"; only "should" or the base form is used.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "will" is not used after "lest".

 

NOTE

 

• Walk carefully lest you should slip, Save some money lest you should need it later (lest + should + base verb).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The contractor will not be paid the final instalment unless he does not complete the pending repair work.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. unless he completes.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Unless" already means "if … not", so it is never used with another negative word. So "unless he does not complete" must be "unless he completes".

◦ Corrected sentence: The contractor will not be paid the final instalment unless he completes the pending repair work.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "until he does not complete" — "until" also carries a time-based sense and is not paired with a redundant "not" here; it does not give the same conditional meaning as "unless".

 

• Option 3: "without he completes" — "without" is a preposition and is followed by a noun or a gerund, never by a clause with its own subject and finite verb such as "he completes".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "unless" is doubled up with the negative "does not".

 

NOTE

 

• You will fail unless you work hard, She will not get the job unless she qualifies (unless + affirmative verb), and not unless … does not.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The security guard will not open the gate until the visitor does not show a valid identity card.
option_1: unless the visitor does not show
option_2: till the time the visitor does not show
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. until the visitor shows.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Until", like "unless", already carries a negative sense ("up to the time when … not"), so a second negative word is not added. So "until the visitor does not show" must be "until the visitor shows".

◦ Corrected sentence: The security guard will not open the gate until the visitor shows a valid identity card.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "unless the visitor does not show" — "unless" also cannot be paired with a second negative, so this repeats the same error with a different conjunction.

 

• Option 2: "till the time the visitor does not show" — this needlessly lengthens the sentence and still keeps the faulty double negative.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "until … does not" is a double negative.

 

NOTE

 

• Wait until he comes, Do not leave until she calls (until + affirmative verb), and not until he does not come.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The main reason for the traffic jam was because a truck had broken down at the junction.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. was that a truck.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After "the reason … is / was", the conjunction "that" is used, and "because" is not needed, since "reason" already expresses cause. So "was because a truck" must be "was that a truck".

◦ Corrected sentence: The main reason for the traffic jam was that a truck had broken down at the junction.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "was because of a truck" — "because of" is a preposition and would need a noun phrase alone, not the full clause "a truck had broken down" that follows.

 

• Option 3: "was due to a truck" — "due to" is also a preposition and cannot smoothly introduce the following clause with its own subject and verb.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "the reason … is/was because" is a redundant construction.

 

NOTE

 

• The reason for his absence was that he was ill, The reason she left early was that she felt unwell (reason … that), and not the reason … was because.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The auditor expressed no doubt whether the company's accounts had been tampered with.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. that.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After a negative expression such as "no doubt", the conjunction "that" is used, while "whether / if" is used after a positive doubt ("I doubt whether …"). So "no doubt whether" must be "no doubt that".

◦ Corrected sentence: The auditor expressed no doubt that the company's accounts had been tampered with.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "if" — "if" is used to introduce a genuine doubt or a condition, and it does not follow the negative "no doubt".

 

• Option 3: "as if" — this is used for an unreal comparison, and it does not fit after "no doubt".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "whether" does not follow the negative "no doubt".

 

NOTE

 

• There is no doubt that he is guilty; I doubt whether he is guilty (no doubt + that; doubt + whether / if).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The officer asked the clerk that if the file had been forwarded to the head office.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. whether.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In indirect speech, a reporting verb like "asked" is followed directly by "whether" or "if", and "that" is never combined with them. So "that if" must be "whether".

◦ Corrected sentence: The officer asked the clerk whether the file had been forwarded to the head office.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "that whether" — "that" still wrongly precedes "whether", repeating the same fault.

 

• Option 2: "if that" — "that" cannot follow "if" in this reported question either.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "that" is not combined with "if" after "asked".

 

NOTE

 

• She asked me whether I was free, He asked if she had left (asked + whether / if), and not asked that whether, asked that if.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The scholarship is open only to such students ___ have scored above ninety per cent in the board exams.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. as.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Such" is followed by the relative pronoun "as", and not by "who" or "which". So the correct answer is "as".

◦ Complete sentence: The scholarship is open only to such students as have scored above ninety per cent in the board exams.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "who" — "who" is a common relative pronoun for people, but it does not follow "such" in this fixed pattern.

 

• Option 2: "which" — "which" is used for things, and it is also not the relative pronoun that follows "such".

 

• Option 3: "whom" — "whom" is an object relative pronoun, and here a subject relative pronoun is needed after "such".

 

NOTE

 

• such books as are useful, such workers as are sincere (such … as), and not such books which are useful.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

Keep a copy of all the receipts ___ the refund is questioned later by the airline.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. in case.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "In case" is a conjunction and is followed by a clause to show a precaution, while "in case of" is a preposition followed by a noun. Here a clause with a subject and verb follows the blank, so the correct answer is "in case".

◦ Complete sentence: Keep a copy of all the receipts in case the refund is questioned later by the airline.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "in case of" — this is followed by a noun phrase, such as "in case of a dispute", and not by a full clause.

 

• Option 3: "in the case of" — this phrase introduces a specific example or instance and is also followed by a noun, not a clause.

 

• Option 4: "unless" — this gives a condition meaning "if … not", which does not fit the precautionary sense intended here.

 

NOTE

 

• Take an umbrella in case it rains (in case + clause); in case of rain, in case of an emergency (in case of + noun).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

Coastal areas often flood during monsoon, ___ the hilly regions rarely face such problems.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. whereas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Whereas" (or "while") is used to join two clauses that show a clear contrast. Coastal flooding is contrasted with the hilly regions rarely flooding, so the correct answer is "whereas".

◦ Complete sentence: Coastal areas often flood during monsoon, whereas the hilly regions rarely face such problems.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "because" — this gives a reason, and there is no cause-and-effect relationship between the two clauses.

 

• Option 2: "unless" — this gives a condition meaning "if … not", which does not suit two contrasting factual statements.

 

• Option 3: "so that" — this shows a purpose or result, which does not fit the contrast being made here.

 

NOTE

 

• The north is dry, whereas the south is wet, He is calm, while his brother is short-tempered (whereas / while for contrast).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Submit your assignment by Friday evening, however your marks will be deducted for late submission.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. otherwise.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Otherwise" (= if this is not done) shows the consequence of not following an instruction, giving the meaning "if you do not submit by Friday evening". "However" cannot join two independent clauses with a comma in this way. So "however" must be "otherwise".

◦ Corrected sentence: Submit your assignment by Friday evening, otherwise your marks will be deducted for late submission.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "nevertheless" — this means "in spite of that", and it does not carry the conditional sense of "if not".

 

• Option 3: "moreover" — this simply adds another point, and it does not warn of a consequence.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "however" cannot correctly join the two clauses here.

 

NOTE

 

• Hurry up, otherwise you will be late, Revise the chapters, otherwise you will struggle in the exam (otherwise = if not).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

As long as I know, the new branch manager joins duty next Monday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. As far as.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "As far as" (not "as long as") is used with "know", "concerned" or "aware" to limit a statement to one's own knowledge, while "as long as / so long as" is used for a condition or duration. Since the sentence is about the speaker's knowledge, "As long as I know" must be "As far as I know".

◦ Corrected sentence: As far as I know, the new branch manager joins duty next Monday.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "So long as" — this also gives a condition or duration, like "as long as", and it does not fit "know" in this pattern.

 

• Option 2: "As much as" — this shows degree or quantity, and it is not the fixed phrase used with "know".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "as long as" is not used with "know" in this sense.

 

NOTE

 

• As far as I know, he is honest, As far as I am concerned, the plan is fine (as far as + know / concerned / aware); as long as you work hard, so long as you pay on time (as long as / so long as = provided that).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

With the last bus already gone, the passengers had no choice than to wait for the morning train.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. no choice but to wait.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "No choice" and "no alternative" are followed by "but" (meaning "except") with a to-infinitive, and not by "than". So "no choice than to wait" must be "no choice but to wait".

◦ Corrected sentence: With the last bus already gone, the passengers had no choice but to wait for the morning train.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "no other choice than wait" — "than" still does not follow "choice", and the to-infinitive "to wait" is also missing.

 

• Option 3: "no choice but wait" — "but" is used correctly here, but the to-infinitive "to wait" is missing after it.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "than" is wrongly used instead of "but" after "no choice".

 

NOTE

 

• had no choice but to leave, had no alternative but to agree (no choice / alternative + but + to-infinitive).
